# Data Analytics {#sec-data-analytics}

## Spatial Unit Analysis
This section tries to answer: (i) Where and when does demand arise and at which spatial and temporal resolution can a fleet realistically be managed? In addition, it tries to generate further information usable for the ride-hailing platform and the fleet operator.

The data set contains three different spatial encodings for each trip: a community area, a census tract, and a latitude/longitude coordinate pair. Chicago has 77 official community areas and a considerably finer census-tract layer, of which 473 tracts carry valid trip start locations. The community area is a coarse administrative unit, while the census tract is a finer unit. The latitude/longitude coordinate is the centroid of the census tract or, if the tract is suppressed for privacy reasons[@chicago_privacy_story], the centroid of the community area. Scattering every coordinate over the community areas (@fig-coords-community) and over the census tracts (@fig-coords-tract) shows that in the centre of the city the points sit at census tract centroids, resolving fine detail, whereas on the outskirts they collapse onto a sparser set of community area centroids, exactly the pattern the privacy suppression would produce. The privacy suppression is therefore a real limitation for the spatial resolution of the data, and it is not possible to recover the original coordinates. The community area is therefore the most complete (missing only about 7 % of dropoffs) and reliable spatial encoding, while the census tract is only available for less than half of the trips. The coordinate is always present, but it is a centroid rather than a true GPS point, so it does not provide any additional spatial resolution beyond the community area or census tract.

An alternative to the administrative units is a regular H3 hexagon grid, a equal-sized hexagonal area cells independent of the political boundaries. They can be set in different sizes, the higher the resolution, the smaller the cells become. 
There are two ways to fill such a grid, and the centroid encoding is in conflict with both. The direct approach assigns each trip endpoint to the hexagon it falls into. Because the coordinates are a small set of repeated centroids rather than continuous GPS points, the trips pile up on the few cells that happen to contain a centroid and leave the rest empty, increasingly so at finer resolutions and towards the city edge (@fig-hex-community). The alternative is areal interpolation in which the endpoints per community area are distributed across the hexagons in proportion to their geometric overlap. This preserves essentially all endpoints (@fig-areal-weighted), but only by assuming that trips are spread uniformly within a community area, which flattens the outskirts into an artificial homogeneity and blurs where activity actually concentrates.

Comparing the areal-weighted hexagons against the raw community area counts (@fig-trips-community) makes the trade-off concrete: the areal weighting smooths activity out, most visibly around the airport in the north-west, while the census tract choropleth (@fig-trips-tract) offers finer detail but leaves the outskirts barely covered, in the same way the raw hexagon grid does. Neither variant therefore adds spatial information that the centroids do not already carry, as the raw grid inherits their sparsity and the interpolated grid merely replaces that sparsity with a modelling assumption.

Therefore, the community area is adopted as the primary spatial unit for the descriptive analysis, as it is complete, internally consistent with the finer encodings, and free of both the smoothing artefacts of areal weighting and the empty-cell sparsity of a raw hexagon grid. Where finer resolution is genuinely available and useful, the census tract remains a secondary view, taking into account that only half of the data can be used for this and that analysis are less accurate.

In terms of fleet management the community area demand is a valuable metric to orchestrate the amount of taxis needed in a certain area, with predictions being accurate enough and within a reasonably sized area for taxis to operate in.

## Spatial and temporal demand patterns {#sec-spatial-temporal-demand-patterns}

Taking the community area as our main spatial unit,the following section explores how demand varies across space and time for this unit. All maps in this part are drawn as paired choropleths, with pickups on the left and dropoffs on the right, so in addition to the volume, the direction of demand is visible.


It can be seen that demand is highly concentrated in a few areas, with the O'Hare airport in the north-west and the downtown core in the centre of the city being the two main poles as seen in @fig-trips-community.
The remainder of the city is close to empty by comparison.
The paired map (@fig-demand-spatial) also exposes an
asymmetry at O'Hare airport, being near-maximal as a source of pickups but
only moderate as a dropoff destination, suggesting that arriving air passengers take taxis away
from the terminal far more often than departing ones are dropped there. Downtown,
by contrast, is roughly symmetric, both generating and attracting trips. Notably,
Midway, the city's second airport to the south-west, barely registers, so the
airport signal in this dataset is essentially an O'Hare signal. For a fleet
operator this implies supply must be pre-positioned at O'Hare and downtown, and
that vehicles will tend to accumulate downtown-bound out of the airport and need
active rebalancing back. The census tract equivalent (@fig-demand-spatial-tract)
reproduces the same O'Hare asymmetry, with the suppressed periphery emptier still,
consistent with the coverage gap described above.

A hotspot analysis quantifies this picture. Fitting a Gaussian Mixture Model
(GMM) to the pickup and dropoff coordinates, with the number of components
chosen by AIC (K = 15 on both sides) and cross-checked against a
kernel density estimate, decomposes demand into named, ranked components
(@fig-kde-hotspots, @fig-gmm-hotspots, @tbl-hotspot-ranking). O'Hare (21.3 %
of pickups), Near North Side (20.9 %) and the Loop (19.0 %) are the three
largest pickup components. On the dropoff side O'Hare splits into two adjacent
components jointly holding only 4.7 %, giving the pickup-heavy airport
asymmetry a concrete figure. Because the coordinates are area centroids and
not street-level points, the components resolve to community-area precision at
best, and the overlapping 2-sigma ellipses in @fig-gmm-hotspots show that
neighbouring basins such as the Loop and Near North Side share their boundary
region instead of dividing cleanly, a nuance a hard fleet-zoning rule would
miss.

Several things are noteworthy about the temporal distribution.
Collapsing the spatial dimension and keeping time
(@fig-hourly-demand) reveals a daily cycle: demand is negligible
overnight, increases steeply from around 05:00, and peaks at 17:00 before
declining into the night. Pickup and dropoff curves almost coincide as the small
lead–lag between them is merely trip duration shifting dropoffs into slightly
later hours, not a strong directional commuting effect. The 8-hour-block maps
(@fig-block-demand) place this in space: the overnight block (00:00–07:59) is
near-empty everywhere, while the midday and most of all the evening block
concentrate activity on the O'Hare pickup pole and the downtown core. Across the
week (@fig-dow-demand) weekdays are near-identical, but Saturday softens the
O'Hare (airport and business-travel) pole while downtown activity holds up,
consistent with a shift from business to leisure travel. Sunday then recovers the
airport component as travellers return. Seasonally (@fig-month-demand) the
spatial structure is invariant, but overall volume varies over the year.
The monthly total confirms November as the
year's low (@fig-monthly-demand). Finally, the demand geography is rather 
robust on public holidays (@fig-holiday-demand): the airport and downtown poles
persist across all four holiday flags, so typical calendar days rescale demand
rather than relocating it. All of these patterns hold essentially unchanged at
census tract resolution (@fig-hourly-demand-tract, @fig-block-demand-tract,
@fig-dow-demand-tract, @fig-month-demand-tract,
@fig-holiday-demand-tract).

Averaging trip attributes per area separates the
features into two clean groups. The weather variables (temperature, precipitation,
humidity, wind, snow) are essentially uniform across the city, weather is a
temporal signal, not a spatial one, and enters the predictive models on the
time axis rather than as a per-area feature. The trip-economics variables, in
contrast, show a strong spatial gradient (@fig-feature-gradient). Mean fare and
mean trip distance rise toward O'Hare and the outer periphery, while mean speed
falls in the congested core. In short, centrality and trip value move in opposite
directions with short, cheap, slow trips in downtown versus long, expensive, fast trips
from the edges and the airport. For an electric fleet this gradient is doubly
relevant as peripheral and airport trips are not only higher-revenue but also
higher-energy consuming, with direct implications for vehicle range and charging strategy.
The same gradient holds at census tract resolution (@fig-feature-gradient-tract),
confirming it is not an artefact of community area aggregation. The full
19-feature grid at both resolutions, and the day-of-week, block, month and
holiday maps, are provided in Appendix -@sec-appendix.

Lastly, we examine points of interest (POI) as an explanation for *why* demand sits where it does. In previous projects and research, it became clear that POIs are a highly influential factor affecting customers of urban mobility. POI data characterise an area regarding its amenities and services and therefore may explain why people travel to certain areas. 
Before adopting POI as a model input, we verify that the same relationship holds in Chicago. For each of the 77 community areas we sum the eight POI categories (healthcare, education, amenity, leisure, shops, public services, tourism, nature) into a single density measure and plot it against taxi activity, measured as the trip endpoints (pickups plus dropoffs) falling within the area. 
The relationship is clearly positive as the three busiest areas show a strong correlation as seen in @fig-poi-demand. The three busiest areas, the Near North Side, the Loop and O'Hare, are in the top-right corner of the plot. Two conclusions can be made: (i) POI density is an explanatory factor for taxi demand due to the concentration of places worth travelling to, and (ii) POI density is a useful engineered feature for predictive modelling, as it carries genuine signal about a location. The full per-category maps, at both census tract and community area resolution, are provided in Appendix -@sec-appendix (@fig-poi-tract, @fig-poi-community).
One drawback is that the POI snapshot is static, so it can explain where demand is high but not how that changes over time. The association is also correlational, since POI density and taxi demand are both consequences of how the city is built.
